engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Calculation: The LPDO Rule
chess.body: LPDO = Loose Pieces Drop Off. Before every move, scan the board: which of my pieces are undefended? Which of my opponent's pieces are undefended? Undefended pieces are targets for tactics. A simple habit: after finding your move, ask 'does this leave anything undefended?' This alone prevents most blunders.

wisdom.title: Stoic Parenting
wisdom.body: Marcus Aurelius raised children while running an empire. His journal shows he constantly asked: am I reacting or responding? Reacting is automatic. Responding is chosen. The next time your baby cries at 2am, ask yourself: how do I want to respond to this? You always have a choice in the gap between stimulus and response.

book.author: Sam Walton
book.lesson: Sam Walton built the world's largest retailer from a small Arkansas five-and-dime store. His rules: commit to your business; share profits with employees; energise your associates; communicate everything; appreciate associates; celebrate successes; listen to everyone in your company; exceed customers' expectations; control expenses; swim upstream (do the opposite of what everyone else does). The most counterintuitive: Walmart succeeded by treating employees as partners and sharing information and profits broadly, while competitors treated labour as a cost to minimise. Also: Walton flew his own plane to personally visit stores until he was 70.
book.key_quote: The best business intelligence comes from people closest to the customer. Go there yourself and listen.
book.action: Identify someone in your team or organisation who is closest to the customer/problem. Ask them what they're seeing that leadership doesn't know about.
crux: Walton's obsession was the customer's price, and everything else followed from it.
Buy low, stack it high, sell it cheap. Volume compensates for margin.
Rural small towns were dismissed by competitors. That was the opening.
Control costs better than anyone. Cost advantage forgives many mistakes.
Distribution centres came before the stores they served. Logistics was the real business.
Invest early in information systems. Walmart's data infrastructure preceded everyone's.
Share profits with associates and they behave like owners.
Listen to the people on the floor. They talk to customers; you don't.
Swim upstream. Go the other way when everyone agrees.
Every store must be visited. Management by walking around, constantly.
Copy shamelessly from competitors. Walton toured rivals' stores relentlessly.
Exceed expectations, celebrate success, and keep the culture unembarrassed.
Frugality is cultural, not cosmetic — shared hotel rooms while running a Fortune 500 company.
learnings: A cost advantage is a strategy, not an accounting detail.
Infrastructure before expansion, or expansion breaks you.
Frontline staff hold the information leadership needs.
Copying well is faster than inventing badly.
examples: Walmart's hub-and-spoke DCs let it saturate regions competitors couldn't serve profitably.
Walton flew his own plane over towns scouting sites, personally, for years.
Profit-sharing from 1971 turned shelf-stackers into shareholders and cut shrinkage.
adapt: Your cost advantage is the whole stack running on GitHub Actions and Vercel free tiers. Protect it.
Infrastructure before features: fix the position lifecycle before adding another scanner.
Copy shamelessly — study what the good finance pages do, then do it in your voice.
Swim upstream: everyone posts motivational finance. Post the actual numbers, including the losses.

minimalism.title: Buy Once, Cry Once
minimalism.body: Minimalism is not cheapness. One well-made pair of shoes at 4x the price that lasts 10x as long is both cheaper and lighter. Fewer, better beats more, adequate.
minimalism.action: List three things you have replaced more than twice. Buy the good version once.
minimalism.label: Minimalism

etiquette.title: Never Discuss What Someone Earns
etiquette.body: Not theirs, not yours, not a third party's. It creates comparison where none existed and it always travels. Especially in the Gulf, where packages vary enormously by nationality and contract.
etiquette.action: Deflect the next compensation question with warmth, not information.
etiquette.label: Etiquette

stillness.title: Desire Is The Contract
stillness.body: Every want you accept is a contract to be unhappy until it is satisfied. Most were installed by advertising, not chosen. Audit the source before signing.
stillness.action: Name one want. Trace where it came from. Decide if it is yours.
stillness.label: Stillness

model.title: Second-Order Thinking
model.body: And then what? Most bad decisions are first-order correct. Price caps look like they help until supply disappears. Ask 'and then what?' three times before committing.
model.action: Take today's main decision three steps forward.
model.label: Mental Model

arabic.use: habeebti to a woman. Used constantly between friends and colleagues. Read the relationship before using it.
arabic.label: Arabic

drill.title: Speak For 60 Seconds, No Filler
drill.body: Record yourself explaining something for a minute with no 'um', 'like', or 'basically'. Silence between sentences reads as authority. Filler reads as uncertainty.
drill.action: Record 60 seconds. Count the filler words. Repeat until zero.
drill.label: Drill

health.title: Protein: 1.6g Per Kg, Minimum
health.body: At 75kg that is 120g daily — far above most intakes. Protein is the one macro where the deficiency is common and the consequence is muscle you cannot easily get back.
health.action: Compute your target. Hit it for one day and see how hard it actually is.
health.label: Health

quote.name: Elon Musk
quote.quote: I think it is possible for ordinary people to choose to be extraordinary.

lesson.lesson: Our greatest glory is not in never falling, but in rising every time we fall.

case.title: Zoho: The Anti-VC Playbook
case.story: Zoho has never taken VC money. Sridhar Vembu built a $1B+ business on profitability, not funding. Employees in rural India, $0 in advertising spend.
case.lesson: You don't need venture capital to build a great company. Profitable growth beats loss-funded growth in the long run.

fpna.title: Zero-Based Budgeting
fpna.body: Start every budget from ₹0. Justify every line. Cuts 15–30% bloat in most orgs.

cfo.title: CFO Step 2: Investor Relations
cfo.body: Listed company CFOs speak to markets quarterly. Practice presenting results: 'Revenue grew 18% YoY driven by X. EBITDA margin expanded 200bps due to Y. FY26 guidance: Z.' Short, precise, numbers-first. Record yourself.

money_hack.title: Term Insurance First
money_hack.body: ₹1Cr term insurance (₹10–15K/year at 25). Non-negotiable. Buy this before any investment.

dubai.title: The cost side nobody models
dubai.body: Housing is paid annually up front in Dubai, or quarterly at a premium. Schooling runs AED 25–60K per child per year. Health insurance is mandatory and usually covered. Add a AED 40–60K first-year setup cost before the savings maths works.
dubai.targets: Sharjah rent is roughly half of Dubai's. The commute costs you 90 minutes a day.
dubai.action: Year-one net savings, not monthly salary. They are very different numbers.

desk.productivity: Batch similar tasks. Answer all messages in one sitting.

father.title: Narrate what you are doing
father.do: Talk through ordinary actions out loud while she watches — 'I am pouring the water, now it is warm.'
father.why: At 7 months she is mapping sound to meaning long before she can speak. Volume of directed speech is the single best-evidenced predictor of later vocabulary. Passive audio does not count; it has to be you, to her.

father.title: Read the same book again
father.do: Read one board book daily, the same one, for a week. Point at the same picture each time.
father.why: Repetition is how infants build prediction. The boredom is yours, not hers — she is learning that symbols hold steady meaning.

life_wisdom.teaching: Reality has more facets than any single viewpoint can hold. The classic image is blind men describing an elephant — each is accurate and each is incomplete.
life_wisdom.apply: In a disagreement, state the other person's position better than they did before you argue against it. If you cannot, you have not understood it yet.

life_wisdom.teaching: The first noble truth is not 'life is suffering' but that conditioned things do not stay satisfying. The promotion satisfies briefly, then resets.
life_wisdom.apply: Before chasing the next milestone, name honestly what the last one actually changed and for how long. Then decide if you still want it.

vocab.example: A cursory review would not have caught this.
vocab.note: Useful for defending the depth of your own work, or flagging the shallowness of someone else's.

vocab.example: The stock count corroborates the system balance.
vocab.note: Independence is the point. Two reports from the same system do not corroborate anything.

speaking.title: Answer, then stop
speaking.drill: Ask yourself an interview question, answer it, and physically close your mouth. Count three seconds before adding anything.
speaking.why: Over-explaining after a complete answer is the most common interview mistake at senior level. The silence is theirs to fill.

interview_tech.q: Sales per square foot is falling but total sales are rising. Diagnose it.
interview_tech.a: You are adding space faster than sales. That is not automatically wrong — new stores ramp, so a growth phase depresses the average mechanically. Split the estate: stores open more than 24 months versus less. If mature-store density is also falling, you have a genuine productivity problem — likely range, pricing, or footfall. If mature density is flat or up and only the blended number falls, it is a mix effect and it corrects as the new stores mature. Never let a board see the blended number alone.

interview_tech.q: Describe the difference between a cash flow forecast and a liquidity plan.
interview_tech.a: The forecast is your best estimate of receipts and payments. The liquidity plan is what you do if the forecast is wrong — committed facilities, uncommitted lines, the order in which you would draw them, what you would stop spending, and how quickly you could release working capital. Boards ask for the forecast; the CFO's real job is the plan. Stress it: what happens to cash if sales fall 20% for two quarters while committed rent and payroll continue.

interview_soft.q: Why do you want to be a CFO, and why in retail?
interview_soft.a: Structure: motive, evidence, specificity. Weak answers say 'growth' and 'leadership'. Strong answer names the work: 'I want the seat where capital allocation is decided, not just reported. In FP&A I model the store investment case; the CFO decides which twelve of thirty get built. Retail because the feedback loop is daily — you see whether the decision worked in the sales line the next week, which is not true in most industries.' Then one proof point with a number attached.

interview_soft.q: How do you build a finance team, and how do you handle an underperformer?
interview_soft.a: Building: hire for one clear gap, not a generalist; define what good looks like in writing before the first review, not after. Underperformance: the honest answer is that you probably waited too long once, and learned from it. Structure — early specific feedback with examples, an agreed plan with dates, documented check-ins, and a decision at the end of it either way. The failure mode they are probing for is a manager who avoids the conversation and lets the team carry someone for a year.
